newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - Sept 27.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - Sept 27.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
DAILY TELEGRAPH
-- JARDINE FLEMING CHAIRMAN QUITS

Alan Smith, chairman of Hong Kong's oldest merchant bank, Jardine Fleming, has resigned less than a month after it was ordered to pay 12 million stg compensation and fined because one of its top fund managers had diverted profitable shares trades to his own personal account. He is to be replaced by the group's managing director Henry Strutt. In a statement Mr Smith was quoted as saying: "With the restructuring in place, I have decided that it is an appropriate time for me to step down."
-- CRISIS TALKS AT SR GENT AFTER 14 MILLION STG PROVISION

SR Gent, the clothing manufacturer and supplier to Marks and Spencer, has disclosed it is in crisis talks with its bankers, prompting its shares to plunge. Gent is close to breaching its banking covenants after being forced to take a 14 million stg provision to close its Clothing Barn chain of seven stores which sell surplus clothing from its South Yorkshire factories. One of the company's major banks is Midland and Michael Stakol, chief executive, has declined to comment on the size of its borrowing now.
-- ASDA CLEARS ALKA SELTZER STOCKS AFTER COURT DEFEAT

Asda has withdrawn packs of Alka Seltzer from its stores after losing a fight with the High Court against Bayer, the German phamaceuticals group, which makes hangover and upset stomach tablets. Bayer won an injunction against Asda which forced the group to comply with its plans to raise the price of the pack by ten pence stg. Corporate counsel for Asda, Nick Cooper, said he was disappointed with the court ruling.
THE TIMES
-- BT STAKES 1.1 BILLION STG IN FRENCH VENTURE

British Telecom has agreed to pay 1.1 billion stg for a 25 percent stake in Cegetel, a company formed to compete with France Telecom. The investment completes BT's European strategy, designed to give it exposure to the Continent's top markets. BT's chief executive Sir Peter Bonfield said the deal is part of a strategy to make continental Europe part of an extended market. The deal will also bring BT into partnership with Compagnie Generale des Eaux, the water-to-healthcare group, which targeted the telecoms industry as its next growth area.
-- BREWING HELPS GUINNESS TO TOAST RECORD HALF YEAR

Guinness, the drinks group, was helped to a record half-year profit by a strong first-half contribution from its brewing activities. Chairman Tony Greener said that the interim results marked a further step for the group in meeting its objective of growing the business and raising the return to shareholders. The recovery in the Irish beer helped Irish business to lift volumes seven percent.
-- ENGLAND'S FARMERS HARVEST RECORD PROFIT

According to a study by the accountant Deloitte and Touche, farmers in England have had their most profitable year, helped by high prices for produce, world shortages and EU aid payments. However, plummeting wheat and potato prices, and a slump in beef sales, are set to take their toll of these profits. The conditions are still better than in the late 1980s and early 1990s, when agriculture came under severe pressure.
THE GUARDIAN
-- CLARKE URGES ACTION AGAINST DIRTY MONEY

Due to a report pointing at Britain's tough legal and regulatory regime as a role model for other nations, Chancellor Kenneth Clarke has called for a worldwide campaign against money-laundering. He warned Commonwealth finance ministers that increasing cross-border cash flows posed a threat to all member countries. The Financial Action Task Force said recent measures taken by Britain to reduce the number of hiding places for money raised through criminal activity had set a new world standard.
-- UNIONS UP MINIMUM-WAGE CLAIM

The most powerful unions, including Unison and NUM, are set to demand an increase in a national minimum wage from 4.26 stg an hour to 4.41 stg, basing these figures on a formula based on official average earnings. The TUC has not yet adopted a specific wage floor and some other unions have suggested a lower rate, of up to four pounds stg. The Labour Party are unlikely to give a committment to the unions over a specific level at next week's conference, with the leadership keenly aware of industry's resistance to a statutory basic wage.
-- INVESCO IN MUTUAL TALKS WITH US AIM

The independent fund management group, Invesco, is in talks with one of America's biggest mutual funds, Aim Management, about a possible "business combination". Invesco said no definitive agreement had been reached and that a further announcement would be made. This follows the speculation that Invesco is seeking to buy Aim for 1.2 billion stg. City analysts welcomed the news, pointing to the complementary nature of the two businesses.
THE INDEPENDENT
-- AEA SHARES ROAR UP TO 323 PENCE

Shares in AEA Technology, the engineering and consultancy arm of the Atomic Energy Authority and the last state asset to be sold before the General Election, have raced to a 15 percent premium on the first day of dealing. AEA's chief executive Peter Watson rejected suggestions the company had been sold too cheaply. The offer to intermediaries, brokers through whom private investors had to apply for their shares, was six times oversubscribed.
-- IMF GUARANTEES TO CUT DEBT BURDEN OF POOR NATIONS

The International Monetary Fund has said plans to reduce the burden of debt repayments on some of the world's poorest nations would go ahead as soon as possible. IMF's managing director Michel Camdessus, said that there was a strong desire to go ahead with the plan. There is still uncertainty about how the initiative will be financed. The IMF claims a four-year gap in the funds available for its contribution will be met by additional contributions from individual member countries.
-- LABOUR CRITICISED OVER CORPORATE GOVERNANCE

The National Association of Pension Funds have launched an attack on the Labour Party over proposals for reforming the way companies are run. The NAPF rejected plans for a standing commission on corporate governance and said suggestions for compulsory voting by institutions at company meetings would create more problems than it would solve. The Association also dismissed the concept of stakeholding, which holds that directors are accountable to wider interests such as employees, customers and suppliers.
